newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: LABOUR THREATENS ACTION ON S.AFRICAN CONSTITUTION.
newsitem.headline: LABOUR THREATENS ACTION ON S.AFRICAN CONSTITUTION.

text.p: South Africa's largest trade union federation on Thursday accused white-led parties of negotiating in bad faith and threatened union action to defend the constitutional tilt towards worker rights.

Neil Coleman, the Congress of South African Trade Unions' lobbyist at parliament, told reporters that National Party and Democratic Party proposals to amend a rejected labour relations clause of the draft constitution sought to undermine hard-won union rights.
"They're trying to reintroduce something that they know is unacceptable and it really is extremely provocative," he said.

"The message (from Cosatu) is to call on members to keep a close watch on the process and to remain ready to react to a call by the leadership of the federation to defend the positions won during the constitutional negotiations," he said.
Coleman declined to say whether the federation would resort to strike action to defend a constitutional right to strike that is not linked to an employer's right to lock out strikers.
The NP and DP have proposed amendments to a draft constitution partly rejected by the Constitutional Court which could reopen a bitter autumn debate about lock-out rights.

Constitution writers declined to include a lock-out provision in their blueprint for post-apartheid rule, but declared the Labour Relations Act which guarantees a limited lock-out right immune to constitutional challenge.
The Constitutional Court ruled that all law should be subject to constitutional challenge.

The NP and DP endorsed a proposal to entrench an employer's right to collective bargaining, but added a reference to the "collective...exercise of economic power" by employers as a balance against the entrenched right to strike.

"It would entrench not only the lock out, but other action. The experts say it is a camouflaged way of introducing the lock out, which has been decisively rejected by the Constitutional Court," Coleman said.
"The court recognised that there is an inequality of power between the parties and that therefore the right to strike was not equal to the right to lock out."
A sub-committee looking at w a new labour relations clause.
Parties agreed to meet privately on Friday to explore ways to resolve the conflict, which should be settled by October 11.
